name: Thuan Thien Sword
powers: Granted victory over the Ming invaders
description: Thuan Thien, the Sword of Heaven's Will, is the magic blade given to the farmer-king Le Loi during his revolt against the Ming occupation of Dai Viet in the fifteenth century, when the golden turtle god Kim Qui surfaced from the waters to present it. With the sword Le Loi's army defeated the Ming and he founded the Later Le dynasty, ruling as the national hero of Vietnamese independence. After the victory, when the king was boating on the lake in Hanoi, the great turtle rose again and seized the sword, returning it to its divine owner, and the lake was renamed Hoan Kiem, the Lake of the Returned Sword. The story is told in the fifteenth-century Lam Son thuc luc chronicle and is a centrepiece of Vietnamese national identity, and the island pagoda Ngoc Son on the lake commemorates the event. Thuan Thien is also celebrated in the legend of the turtle that bore the sword, and the blade remains the emblem of Vietnam's struggle for independence.

name: Betel and Areca Tray
powers: Foundation of hospitality and marriage ritual
description: The betel and areca tray is the lacquered brass container that carries betel leaves, areca nut, and lime, the essential offering of Vietnamese hospitality, courtship, and marriage ritual. In the founding legend two twin brothers, Cao and Lang, loved the same woman; when the woman married Cao, Lang wandered away and died by a stream, and Cao, grieving, drowned himself; the woman then died too. The gods transformed the brothers into the areca tree and the betel vine that climbs it, and the woman into the limestone that binds their flavour, so that the chewing of betel and areca joins the three together in eternal kinship. The tray is presented at weddings as a symbol of this bond, offered to guests as a mark of respect, and placed before ancestors during rites. In village custom the exchange of betel seals a promise, and the phrase 'to invite betel' still means to ask for a daughter's hand. The tray is among the most symbolic household objects of Vietnamese culture.
source: Betel and areca legend; folk custom

name: The Jade Emperor's Gong
powers: Summoned rain when struck by the frog
description: The Jade Emperor's gong is the bronze instrument of a Vietnamese folk tale in which a frog leads a deputation of animals to heaven to complain that rain never falls. Because the frog croaks so loudly, the Jade Emperor hears it above the clouds and summons the delegation; the frog is granted the power to control rain, and to this day the croaking of frogs is said to warn of coming rain. In some tellings the frog beats the Jade Emperor's own bronze gong to announce the arrival of the animals, or to wake the sleepy god, and the tale survives chiefly through oral retellings across the Red River delta. The gong is a story element rather than a documented artifact, and it belongs to the large Vietnamese cycle of pourquoi tales about the order of the natural world. The story explains both the frog's croak and the dragon's water-taming work, and it is one of the most retold animal tales in the Vietnamese classroom.

name: Co Loa Crossbow
description: The magic crossbow of Co Loa is the weapon of An Duong Vuong, the legendary king of the Au Lac kingdom, whose trigger was forged from the golden claw of Kim Qui, the golden turtle god, and which could kill thousands of men with a single shot. The king built the spiral citadel of Co Loa with the turtle's help, but his defence was undone by his own daughter: My Chau, newly married to the spy Trong Thuy of the northern enemy, showed him the secret of the trigger, and the enemy stole it, the citadel fell, and An Duong Vuong fled with his daughter. Learning of the betrayal, the king beheaded My Chau, and her blood is said to have turned into pearls. The story is told in the Lĩnh Nam chích quái and the Dai Viet su ky toan thu, and it is one of the foundational legends of Vietnamese national memory, the site at Co Loa near Hanoi being among the oldest archaeological monuments of the country.

name: The Bayon Smile
powers: The king's watchful presence over the kingdom
description: The Bayon smile is the serene, downcast smile of the great stone face-towers of the Bayon temple at Angkor Thom, built in the twelfth century under the Buddhist king Jayavarman VII. Scores of colossal faces, each several metres high, gaze from the four sides of the towers, and scholars debate whether they portray the king himself, the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, or the fusion of the two in the king's consecrated image. Khmer legend and local tradition read the many faces as the king's presence watching over his kingdom from every direction, a gaze both compassionate and sovereign. The temple was the state temple of Jayavarman's capital, and its face-towers combine Mahayana Buddhist devotion with the Khmer tradition of the devaraja, the god-king. The Bayon smile has become the emblem of Angkor and of Cambodian identity, appearing on the national flag and in art worldwide as an image of serene royal power.

name: The Four White Umbrellas
powers: Emblems of the right to rule granted from above
description: The four white umbrellas are the tiered white standards that the Burmese chronicles place among the regalia of the first kings of the Bagan and later dynasties, emblems of the right to rule granted from above. In the creation tale of kingship, the story of Thagya Min and the first king, the white umbrella is the mark of the king chosen by heaven, and the number of umbrellas carried over a ruler marked his rank, with the great white umbrella of the king symbolizing the highest authority. The image of the king as the bearer of the white umbrella survives in the Hmannan Yazawin chronicle and in the coronation imagery of the Burmese court, and the umbrella standard still crowns Burmese pagodas and throne halls as marks of sacred authority. The same iconography is shared with Thailand and Laos, where the tiered white parasol is the emblem of the Buddhist king. The four umbrellas bind earthly sovereignty to the blessing of the nats, the spirits who watch over the realm.

name: The Relic of That Phanom
powers: Focus of veneration; guardian presence of the Mekong
description: The relic of That Phanom is a sacred relic of the Buddha's breastbone enshrined in the great stupa of That Phanom on the Mekong, the most revered chedi of Laos and northeastern Thailand. Lao legend holds that two monks carried the relic to the site and that a naga king, Phanya Sithan, invited the company and guarded the shrine, binding the sacred monument to the serpentine protectors of the river; the date of the enshrinement is given as the Year of the Goat and celebrated every year at the That Phanom festival. The stupa itself, a tall pyramidal chedi gilded in gold, was severely damaged by a storm in 1975 and rebuilt with a national campaign, and it remains a pilgrimage centre drawing people from both banks of the Mekong. The relic is venerated as a palladium of the region, and its festival in the twelfth lunar month, the Bun Pha That Phanom, is one of the great gatherings of Lao Buddhism. The connection of the shrine to the naga reflects the deep riverine religion of the Mekong valley.

name: Khaen
powers: Voice of lam song and festival celebration
description: The khaen is the free-reed mouth organ of Laos, built from rows of bamboo tubes bound around a wooden wind-chest, whose drone-and-melody sound is the soul of the Lao folk song called lam. The player breathes in and out through a single mouth-hole while covering the finger-holes of the tubes, producing the interlocking melody and drone that lam singers improvise against, and the instrument accompanies courtship, festivals, and ritual across Laos and northeastern Thailand. Lao tradition says that the khaen shaped the speech and poetry of the people, and the instrument is central to the great courtship tradition of the khap and lam. In the origin legend the khaen was first made by a man who wanted to imitate the sound of the wind in the bamboo, and its seven-note scale is regarded as the seed of Lao musical thought. UNESCO has inscribed the khaen playing of the Lao people as intangible cultural heritage, and the instrument remains the emblem of Lao national music.
